en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Ārāmavagga 51. The Training Rule on Entering a Garden Monastery.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were engaged in robe-making work while wearing only a single robe in a village residence.
Some bhikkhunīs entered the monastery without asking for permission and approached those bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How indeed can nuns enter the monastery without having asked for permission?
… [as before] … “Is it true, monks, that nuns enter the monastery without having asked for permission?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can bhikkhunīs enter the monastery without having asked for permission?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule:
"Whichever nun enters a monastery without having asked permission, there is an offense of expiation.
Thus was this training rule for the nuns laid down by the Blessed One.
Now at that time, those monks departed from that monastery.
The bhikkhunīs, thinking, “The masters have departed,” did not go to the monastery.
Then those monks returned once more to that monastery.
The bhikkhunīs, hearing that “the noble ladies have arrived,” entered the monastery after taking leave and approached those bhikkhus.
Having approached and paid homage to those bhikkhus, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those bhikkhunīs said to those bhikkhus: “Sisters, why did you neither sweep the monastery nor set out drinking water and water for washing?”
“Venerable ladies, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One: ‘One must not enter a monastery without having asked permission.
That is why we did not come.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] …
“Monks, I allow you to enter the monastery after having asked permission from a monk who is present.
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule:
‘If any nun should enter the monastery without asking permission from a monk who is present, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
Thus this training rule for the bhikkhunīs was laid down by the Blessed One.
Now at that time, those bhikkhus, having departed from that residence, returned to that same residence again.
The bhikkhunīs, thinking, "The masters have departed," entered the monastery without asking permission.
They became anxious, thinking: “A training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One: ‘One must not enter a monastery without having asked permission from a monk who is present.
Yet we have entered the monastery without asking permission from a monk who was present.
Have we perhaps fallen into an offense entailing confession (pācittiya)? …pe…
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“…And furthermore, bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule as follows—”
“Whichever nun, however, knowingly enters a monastery containing monks without having asked permission, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whichever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the type of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Knows" means:
One knows it oneself, or others inform one of it, or they inform those who do.
A monastery with monks is called "sabhikkhu" (with monks),
even if there are only monks staying at the foot of a tree.
"Should enter the monastery without having asked for permission":
for one who crosses the boundary of an enclosed monastery without having asked a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or an ārāmika for permission, there is an offense of pācittiya.
For one who enters the precincts of an unenclosed monastery, there is an offense of pācittiya.

If there are monks present, and she perceives that there are monks present, and she enters the monastery without asking permission of a monk who is there, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If there are monks present, but she is unsure of it, and she enters the monastery without asking permission of a monk who is there, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If there are monks present, but she perceives that there are no monks present, and she enters the monastery without asking permission of a monk who is there, there is no offense.
If there are no monks, but one perceives that there are monks, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If there are no monks, but one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If there are no monks, and one perceives that there are no monks, there is no offense.
There is no offense if he enters after having asked permission of a monk who is present,
or if he enters without asking permission of a monk who is absent.
She goes looking around;
she goes to where the bhikkhunīs have assembled;
there is a path through the monastery.
For one who is ill,
in cases of distress,
for one who is insane,
"By one who is a first offender":
thus ends the first training rule.
